claim: SEMI E5 (SECS-II) defines a library of standard messages for the most typical IC-manufacturing activities and lets equipment makers define equipment-specific messages for activities the standard messages do not cover.
evidence: "The messages defined in the Standard support the most typical activities required for IC manufacturing" ... "The Standard also provides for the definition of equipment-specific messages to support those activities not covered by the standard messages" (SEMI store abstract, para 1.1.3)

claim: SEMI E37 (HSMS) is the TCP/IP-based way of carrying SECS messages between computers in a fab, intended as a higher-speed alternative to the older serial SECS-I (SEMI E4) link.
evidence: "HSMS is intended as an alternative to SEMI E4 (SECS-I) for applications where higher speed communication is needed" ... "for applications where TCP/IP is preferred over OSI" ... "HSMS defines a communication interface suitable for the exchange of messages between computers in a semiconductor factory" (SEMI store abstract)

claim: Cimetrix (PDF Solutions) explains SEMI equipment communication as three layers: a transport protocol (SECS-I or HSMS) like a phone line, a message format (SECS-II) like a shared language, and functionality standards (GEM/GEM300) that give the messages context.
evidence: "Transport Protocol Standards (SECS-I or HSMS) are analogous to the phone system used during the telephone conversation" ... "Message Format Standards (SECS-II) are analogous to the language the speakers use" ... "Specific Functionality Standards (GEM/GEM300) are analogous to the subject of a telephone conversation" (GEM300 white paper, section 2 Communication Layers)

claim: SEMI E40 (Processing Management) standardises how a factory host tells equipment which processing (a process job: a recipe applied to specified material) to run; it includes only a simple tuning mechanism for limited feedforward/feedback between steps and is not expected to meet all closed-loop control needs.
evidence: "This Standard specifies the application of the appropriate processing to specified material received at the processing agent" ... "A simple tuning mechanism is provided for limited feedforward and feedback control between process steps" ... "This is not expected to satisfy all closed loop control requirements" (SEMI store abstract, 1.2 and 2.3)

claim: In GEM300 usage a Process Job defines which process program (recipe) to run on a specified set of substrates, optionally with parameters that configure the recipe.
evidence: "A Process Job specifies the processing to be applied to the material by a resource" ... "a Process Job defines which process program (recipe) to use when processing a specified set of substrates" ... "A process job may also include parameters to configure the process program" (GEM300 white paper, 5.3 SEMI E40)

claim: SEMI E94 (Control Job Management) gives the factory host services to coordinate processing and disposition of material on production equipment; a control job is a unit of work for one or more carriers made up of one or more process jobs.
evidence: "These services provide capabilities for the host to coordinate processing and disposition of materials on production equipment" ... "A control job defines a unit of work for one or more carriers" ... "E94 must be used in conjunction with the E40 Standard for Processing Management" (SEMI E94 store abstract 1.1; GEM300 white paper 5.6)

claim: SEMI E87 (Carrier Management) standardises host-equipment communication while automated or manual carrier transfers to and from a tool (and its internal buffer) are coordinated, executed and completed.
evidence: "This Specification provides a standardized behavior for host view communication with production equipment during the coordination, execution, and completion of automated and manual carrier transfers to and from the equipment and, if it exists, its internal buffer space" (SEMI store abstract 1.1)

claim: Under SEMI E87 a carrier's wafers may not be processed until the carrier ID and slot map (which slots hold wafers) have been verified; each load port can be configured for automatic AMHS delivery or manual loading.
evidence: "E87 includes provisions for reserving a specific load port, verifying carrier IDs, and even verifying slot maps" ... "Until a carrier ID and slot map are verified, the carrier contents may not be processed" ... "A load port may be configured for automatic AMHS operation or manual loading" (GEM300 white paper 5.4)

claim: SEMI E90 (Substrate Tracking) splits responsibility: the factory system manages information about each substrate, while the equipment must provide services to track substrates while they are inside it; a later revision lets the factory confirm each substrate ID before processing.
evidence: "Essentially, information about substrates is managed by the factory system, while the equipment is required to provide the services for the substrate information management" ... "E90 was enhanced to allow the factory to confirm the ID of each substrate before it is processed" (SEMI E90 store abstract 2.1; GEM300 white paper 5.5)

claim: SEMI E116 (Equipment Performance Tracking) has equipment report its own state changes, time in state and blocked reasons to the host without operator or host input, which SEMI says is essential in 300 mm fabs with minimal manual interaction; combined with MES data it enables SEMI E10 and E79 metrics.
evidence: "The ability to track equipment performance without user input is essential in 300 mm wafer factories where operational scenarios require minimal manual interaction" ... "when combined with external data from the Manufacturing Execution System (MES), will enable accurate calculation of SEMI E10 states and SEMI E79 metrics" (SEMI store abstract 1.1-1.3)

claim: SEMI E10 defines six mutually exclusive basic equipment states (one, unscheduled downtime, is the "failed" state) and standard reliability, availability, maintainability and utilization metrics such as MTBF and MTTR.
evidence: "This Specification defines six mutually exclusive, basic equipment states" ... "One equipment state called the unscheduled downtime state (UDT) defines a" ... "Including mean time between failures (MTBF)" ... "Including mean time to repair (MTTR)" (SEMI store abstract 2.1-2.3)

claim: SEMI E10 was originally published in 1986 and is described on the SEMI site as one of the most widely used SEMI standards.
evidence: "Originally published in 1986, SEMI E10" ... "is one of the most widely used SEMI standards" (semi.org article on E10 revision)

claim: SEMI E10 is used as the common basis for setting equipment performance requirements in purchase and service negotiations between chipmakers and tool suppliers, and feeds cost-of-ownership (E35), OEE (E79) and factory productivity (E124) metrics.
evidence: "SEMI E10 supports supplier-user relationships by providing a basis to establish equipment performance requirements during purchase and service negotiations" ... "Overall Equipment Efficiency (OEE) defined in SEMI E79" (semi.org article on E10 revision)
notes: Article author is a consultant (Productivity Management Associates), published on semi.org.

claim: The GEM300 suite (defined in SEMI E192) builds on SECS-II/HSMS and GEM (E30) with E39, E40, E87, E90, E94, E116, E148 and E157 for carrier management, jobs and substrate tracking.
evidence: "As defined in the SEMI E192 standard, the GEM300 suite includes the following SEMI standards" ... "SEMI GEM300 standards (E39, E40, E87, E90, E94, E116, E148, and E157)" (cimetrix.com/gem300; EDA white paper p.3)

claim: PDF Solutions (Cimetrix) states that all 300 mm fabs mandate GEM300 compliance for tools and that GEM300 is increasingly adopted in back-end (assembly/test) operations.
evidence: "All 300 mm semiconductor fabrication facilities mandate that tools comply with GEM300 standards" ... "GEM300 is increasingly being adopted by back-end semiconductor processes" (cimetrix.com/gem300, Introduction)

claim: SEMI E84 defines the parallel I/O signals for handing a wafer carrier between active AMHS equipment (AGV, RGV, OHT) and passive equipment (process and metrology tools, stockers), including error detection and recovery; the factory host does not manage the handoff itself.
evidence: "the active equipment (e.g., AMHS equipment including AGV, RGV and OHT) and the passive equipment (e.g., production equipment including process and metrology equipment; stockers, etc.)" ... "Error indication, detection, and recovery" ... "The factory level controller (i.e., host) does not manage the handoff operation" (SEMI store abstract)

claim: SEMI says fabs depend on standard host-equipment communication because, with many suppliers, protocols and software interactions, custom integrations quickly become complex and costly.
evidence: "With countless suppliers, protocols, and software interactions, custom integrations quickly become complex and costly" (SEMI Smart Manufacturing Standards page, Equipment Communication and Automation Standards Suite)

claim: The SEMI Equipment Data Acquisition (EDA, "Interface A") suite (E120, E125, E128, E132, E134, E138, E164) runs as SOAP/XML web services over HTTP(S) and supplements rather than replaces SECS/GEM, since it has no equipment control features.
evidence: "The main SEMI EDA standards include E120, E125, E128, E132, E134, E138, and E164" ... "The Web Services use SOAP/XML-formatted messages over an HTTP or HTTPS connection to transfer information" ... "EDA does not include features for equipment control or configuration" (Cimetrix EDA white paper p.3)

claim: A key reason fabs adopted Interface A: SECS/GEM implementations typically allow only one host connection, so several data-gathering applications cannot run at once without a sharing layer, whereas EDA supports multiple concurrent clients and is self-describing via E125 metadata.
evidence: "SECS/GEM implementations typically support only one client (host) connection" ... "EDA supports multiple, independent concurrent clients" ... "EDA is self-describing through the E125 metadata standard" (Cimetrix EDA white paper, FAQ)

claim: Since the EDA standards were first released in 2005, chipmakers have written them into automation purchase specifications for 300 mm equipment, and (per Cimetrix) EDA interfaces are available on every equipment type needed for the most advanced processes.
evidence: "Since the initial release of the EDA standards in 2005, IC makers began to include them in their automation purchase specifications for 300mm equipment" ... "EDA interfaces are available on every type of equipment required for the most advanced manufacturing processes" (Cimetrix EDA white paper p.4)

claim: Because EDA standards keep changing, SEMI defined "freeze versions" (Freeze I 1105, adopted 2006; Freeze II 0710); equipment and client must implement the same version to interoperate, so most factory systems must support multiple freeze versions.
evidence: "The industry adopted the initial 1105 Freeze Version (Freeze I) in 2006" ... "Unless the client applications and Equipment are implementing the same version of the EDA standards, they cannot fully communicate" ... "so most factory systems will need to support multiple Freeze Versions" (Cimetrix EDA white paper FAQ p.23)

claim: Interface A data-collection workflow: a client first opens an authenticated session (E132), reads the equipment metadata model (E125) to see what data exists, defines and activates Data Collection Plans (E134), and receives data reports until it deactivates the plans or disconnects, then closes the session.
evidence: "Initially, each client must establish an authenticated session" ... "With this information, the client can define and activate Data Collection Plans" ... "The equipment will then continue to generate Data Collection Reports until the client deactivates the plans or becomes unavailable" (Cimetrix EDA white paper, EDA Client Operations p.18)
notes: Workflow: trigger=engineering/FDC application needs tool data; actor=EDA client (factory data-collection system) and equipment EDA server; input=E125 metadata; decision=which parameters/events/traces to put in the DCP; system=Interface A (E132/E125/E134); output=Data Collection Reports; exception=overload -> E134 performance-status notification (see overload claim).

claim: In Interface A the equipment supplier decides how much data a tool can expose while factory clients decide how much is collected; clients can request enough data to overload the tool's interface computer and slow the tool, so E134 includes a performance-status warning.
evidence: "the equipment supplier determines how much data is available, but the clients determine how much data is gathered and reported" ... "Clients can potentially submit enough data collection requests to overload the equipment" ... "E134 also defines a Performance Status operation to notify consumers of an overload condition" (Cimetrix EDA white paper, 3.4 E134)

claim: Cimetrix notes that fabs expect EDA to expose detailed sensor, actuator and internal control data, and delivering it at the required performance may require redesigning some tools' embedded control systems.
evidence: "factory customers ultimately expect access to much more detailed equipment data" ... "it may be necessary to redesign the embedded control systems of some equipment" (Cimetrix EDA white paper p.3-4)

claim: SEMI E164 (EDA Common Metadata) standardises how equipment metadata is represented under E125 Equipment Self-Description, including the metadata of common 300 mm communication standards, and applies only to production equipment that acts on substrates.
evidence: "defining common representations and conventions of equipment metadata based on SEMI E125 Specification for Equipment Self-Description" ... "This Specification applies only to production equipment that act on substrates" (SEMI store abstract)

claim: PDF Solutions says fabs use data gathered via EDA/Interface A for FDC, run-to-run APC, equipment health monitoring, chamber/tool matching, predictive maintenance and virtual metrology.
evidence: "Factories can use the data gathered through EDA interfaces for FDC, run-to-run advanced process control, equipment health monitoring, chamber/tool matching, predictive maintenance, virtual metrology, diagnostics" (Form 10-K FY2025, Item 1, Cimetrix CIMPortal Plus)

claim: SEMI E183 (RITdb) specifies a data and event sharing and streaming method for semiconductor test: a relational data container for legacy and extended data with provenance via metadata and cryptographic hashing/signing, plus a real-time publish-subscribe messaging system based on an M2M-IoT protocol.
evidence: "This Specification describes a data and event sharing and streaming methodology for semiconductor test and related operations" ... "Provenance of all data is supported via customizable metadata along with cryptographic hashing and signing" ... "a real time publish subscribe event messaging system optimized for semiconductor manufacturing and based on a Machine-to-Machine Internet of Things (M2M-IoT) protocol" (SEMI store abstract)

claim: SEMI says RITdb is not simply a new version of STDF: it also defines real-time messages over MQTT publish-subscribe so test data can be used as it is generated, and is designed so that everything in an STDF file can be represented in a RITdb container.
evidence: "There is an assumption that RITdb is simply a new version of the Standard Test Data Format (STDF) to store test data" ... "RITdb also defines how to send real-time messages over the Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) protocol" ... "RITdb is designed to ensure all information captured in STDF files, plus other data from test operations, can be represented in a RITdb container" (SEMI blog by RITdb task-force leaders)

claim: Work on RITdb began in 2010 and the first RITdb standard, SEMI E183, was first published in November 2021 (revision E183-1121), with a technical revision in January 2023.
evidence: "The RITdb effort started in 2010" ... "SEMI E183-1121 (first published)" ... "SEMI E183-0123 (technical revision)" (SEMI Standards Watch Mar 2022; SEMI store revision history)

claim: SEMI contrasts front-end control, where the MES/host commands each tool point-to-point via SECS/GEM, with test cells, where the tester may be told mid-run to run extra or different tests on the next die based on current conditions, a decision often needed at sub-second speed.
evidence: "In front-end processing, a high-level manager (factory host or MES) makes command and control decisions" ... "the tester may be instructed to do something different for that product/die, such as perform additional or different tests" ... "often at the sub-second level" (SEMI blog, front-end vs test environment)
notes: Workflow (adaptive test): trigger=test-cell condition/result on current die; actor=tester + test-floor system; decision=add/alter tests for next die without changing the base test program; system=RITdb streaming; output=modified test flow; constraint=sub-second latency.

claim: Advantest says semiconductor test analysis has historically been file-based and done offline, taking days or weeks to find and fix issues; its ACS Real-Time Data Infrastructure (launched 2023) aims to turn insights into test decisions within milliseconds.
evidence: "The current file-based approach is performed offline, taking days or even weeks to identify and resolve any issues" ... "automate the process of converting insights into actionable test decisions within milliseconds" (Advantest press release 12 Dec 2023)

claim: Advantest's ACS RTDI platform launched with analytics partners including PDF Solutions (Exensio), proteanTecs and Synopsys (Silicon.da).
evidence: "Said Akar, GM, Exensio Analytics at PDF Solutions" ... "Uzi Baruch, chief strategy officer, proteanTecs" ... "The availability of Synopsys Silicon.da real-time production analytics applications" (Advantest press release 12 Dec 2023, Partner Endorsements)

claim: The Automotive Electronics Council guideline AEC-Q001 defines part average testing (PAT), a statistical method for removing parts with abnormal (outlier) test results from AEC-Q100/Q101 components, using either static limits or dynamic limits recalculated for each lot or wafer.
evidence: "This guideline presents a statistically based method, called part average testing (PAT), for removing parts with abnormal characteristics (outliers)" ... "The dynamic test limits are based on the static limits, but are established for each lot (or wafer in a lot) and continuously modified as each lot (or wafer) is tested" (AEC-Q001 Rev-D, sections 1 and 3.1)

claim: Under AEC-Q001, static PAT limits must be reviewed and updated with current data during the first 6 months of production or at least 8 wafer lots, whichever comes first.
evidence: "The static PAT limits shall be reviewed and updated as required using current data during the first 6 months of production or at least 8 wafer lots, whichever occurs first" (AEC-Q001 Rev-D, 3.1.1.1)

claim: SEMI E187 sets baseline cybersecurity requirements (operating-system support, network security, endpoint protection, security monitoring) for Windows/Linux computers in fab production equipment and AMHS; it excludes PLCs and SCADA devices.
evidence: "This Standard addresses required measures for cybersecurity in the design, operation, and maintenance of semiconductor production equipment and automated material handling system" ... "This Standard does not apply to computing devices of programmable logic controllers (PLCs), supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA)" (SEMI store abstract)

claim: SEMI cites a 2018 ransomware incident that forced a major foundry to pause production; its first cybersecurity standards, E187 (led by TSMC and ITRI) and E188 on malware-free equipment integration (led by Intel and Cimetrix), were published in 2022.
evidence: "a major foundry was forced to pause production to investigate machines infected by ransomware in 2018" ... "led by Leon Chang (TSMC) and Ares Cho (ITRI), developed E187" ... "Led by Ryan Bond of Intel and Richard Howard of Cimetrix" (SEMI Standards Watch, March 2022)

evidence: "The semiconductor industry generates terabytes of data daily" ... "This translates to petabytes of data that need to be stored, managed, and analyzed, often requiring dedicated data centers" (blog 'Semiconductor Manufacturing Data 101', The Scale of Semiconductor Data)
